procedural_history.impugned_order: Order by the Lieutenant Governor of Goa to leave India.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The order was challenged in Criminal Revision Petition No. 55 of 1966 at the Judicial Commissioner Court, Goa, Daman and Diu. The petition was dismissed on August 7, 1967.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Rev. Father Monteiro appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the order of the Judicial Commissioner, Goa dated August 7, 1967.

issue.issue_text: Whether the protection against deportation under Article 49 of the Geneva Convention continues to apply to the appellant on the ground that Goa remains 'occupied territory' under Article 47, despite its annexation by India.

facts: The appellant, a resident of Goa, chose to retain his Portuguese nationality after India's annexation of the territory.
He was granted a temporary residential permit, which he allowed to expire without seeking renewal.
The Lieutenant Governor of Goa ordered him to leave India, and he was prosecuted and convicted for disobeying this order.
The appellant argued that he was a 'protected person' under the Geneva Conventions and that Goa remained 'occupied territory' despite the annexation.
law: Article 47 of the Fourth Geneva Convention states that protected persons in an occupied territory cannot be deprived of the benefits of the Convention by any change introduced by the occupation, including the annexation of the territory.
Article 49 of the same Convention forbids the deportation of protected persons from occupied territory.
The Geneva Conventions Act of 1960 incorporated these conventions into Indian law.
application: The Supreme Court distinguished between a 'premature annexation' (which occurs while a conflict is ongoing) and a 'true annexation' that follows a complete conquest and subjugation.
The Court reasoned that Article 47 was intended to apply only to 'premature annexations' to prevent an occupying power from circumventing its obligations during a conflict.
It found that the military action in Goa was swift, lasting only a few hours with no resistance, and was immediately followed by a complete annexation and subjugation on December 20, 1961.
This constituted a 'true annexation,' which ended the state of 'occupation' as understood in the Convention.
Because the occupation had ceased, the protections of the Geneva Conventions, including the prohibition on deportation in Article 49, no longer applied to the appellant.
The Court also noted that the Geneva Conventions Act did not grant individuals a specific right or remedy to enforce the Conventions against the government in a domestic court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's claim, holding that the 'occupation' of Goa had ended with its complete and 'true annexation' by India. Therefore, Goa was no longer 'occupied territory' under the meaning of the Geneva Convention, and the appellant was not entitled to the protection against deportation provided by Article 49.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Foreigners Act and orders passed thereunder could be legally applied to the appellant, who had declared Portuguese nationality, to order his deportation.

facts: The appellant was a resident of Goa, which was annexed by India.
Following the annexation, he was given a choice of nationality and he declared himself to be of Portuguese nationality.
As a foreigner, he was granted a temporary residential permit to stay in India, which he did not renew after it expired.
He was subsequently ordered to leave India by the Lt. Governor of Goa under the Foreigners Act.
He disobeyed the order and was prosecuted and convicted.
law: The Court cited the cardinal principle of international law that every state has territorial supremacy.
This supremacy grants a state the legal right and competence to exclude aliens from its territory at its discretion.
A state can make laws to regulate the entry, residence, and eviction of aliens within its territory.
application: The Court reasoned that by choosing to retain his Portuguese nationality, the appellant became an alien in India.
As an alien, his right to reside in India was not absolute but was subject to the laws of India, specifically the Foreigners Act.
His stay was conditional upon having a valid permit. Once his permit expired, the government was within its legal rights to order his deportation.
The appellant's arguments based on the Geneva Conventions were dismissed, as the court held that his status was that of a foreigner by his own choice, subject to domestic law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the government's position, holding that the Foreigners Act and the deportation order were legally and competently applied to the appellant. Because he had voluntarily chosen to be a foreigner, he was subject to India's sovereign right to regulate the residence and eviction of aliens.

issue.issue_text: Whether the acquisition of territory by force of arms can confer a valid title in international law after the United Nations Charter.

facts: The case involved a territory that was taken over after a military engagement lasting only a few hours, with no subsequent resistance.
A complete annexation of the territory occurred on December 20, 1961, immediately following the military action.
The parties in the case did not dispute that the annexation itself was lawful.
law: The Court acknowledged the United Nations Charter's prohibition on using force against the territorial integrity of other states (Art. 2 para 4).
However, the Court observed that despite the Charter, state practice since World War II has shown that the transfer of title to territory by conquest is still recognized in international law.
Citing legal scholars, the Court noted the principle that if a conqueror is in full and uncontested possession of a territory, this factual reality can lead to a valid title.

The Court drew a distinction between a temporary "belligerent occupation" and a full "annexation," where the occupying power acquires uncontested sovereignty and a de jure right to administer the territory.
application: The Court determined that the situation was not a prolonged "belligerent occupation" but a "true annexation by conquest and subjugation."
It found that the annexation followed the military action so closely that there was no real gap between the two events.

Because the annexation was complete, uncontested, and its lawfulness was conceded, the Court concluded that the state of "occupation" (in the sense relevant to the Geneva Conventions) had ceased on December 20, 1961.
The Court reasoned that when a conflict is over and annexation is complete, it has the effect of creating a valid title to the territory.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the idea that the acquisition of territory by force cannot confer a valid title after the UN Charter. It held that international law and state practice still recognize that a complete and uncontested conquest, resulting in a true annexation, can create a valid title to the territory.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the protection against deportation under Article 49 of the Geneva Convention continues to apply to the appellant on the ground that Goa remains 'occupied territory' under Article 47, despite its annexation by India.
appellant_arguments: The Geneva Conventions continue to apply because Goa remains an 'occupied territory' in International Law as it had neither been ceded, nor had the Occupying Power (India) withdrawn.
As a result of Goa's status as an occupied territory, the protection of Articles 47 and 49 of the Geneva Convention continued to be available to the appellant.
respondent_arguments: Occupation by armed forces (belligerent occupation) comes to an end by conquest followed by subjugation.
The Geneva Conventions ceased to apply after December 20, 1961, when the conquest was complete.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Foreigners Act and orders passed thereunder could be legally applied to the appellant, who had declared Portuguese nationality, to order his deportation.
appellant_arguments: The appellant is protected by the Geneva Conventions, and therefore by disobeying the deportation order issued under the Foreigners Act, he did not commit any offence.
respondent_arguments: The appellant refused Indian nationality and retained his Portuguese nationality, making him a foreigner.
As a Portuguese national, he could only stay in India with a valid permit.
Since he did not have a valid permit, he was rightly prosecuted under the Foreigners Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the acquisition of territory by force of arms can confer a valid title in international law after the United Nations Charter.
appellant_arguments: After the United Nations Charter, the acquisition of territory by force of arms cannot confer a valid title in International Law.
India's annexation was only legalised internally by a constitutional amendment, but in International Law, the territory remained occupied.
respondent_arguments: Occupation comes to an end by conquest followed by subjugation, which implies that conquest does confer title and changes the legal status of the territory.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A state has the sovereign and discretionary power, arising from its territorial supremacy, to control the reception, residence, and exclusion of aliens through its domestic laws. An alien cannot enforce the provisions of an international convention in a municipal court to challenge such domestic laws, as these conventions do not create a private right of action against the state unless the domestic statute implementing the convention explicitly provides for one.
obiter: The laws of belligerent occupation apply only during the course of actual warfare and do not apply to an occupation after the enemy has been totally defeated.
In international law, the transfer of title to territory by conquest is still recognized.
A territory is considered occupied when it is in fact placed under the authority of a hostile army.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Geneva Conventions ceased to apply to Goa after December 20, 1961, when the conquest by India was complete and the state of belligerent occupation ended. Consequently, the appellant, having chosen to retain his Portuguese nationality, was legally a foreigner subject to Indian domestic law, including the Foreigners Act, and could not invoke the Conventions in a municipal court to prevent his deportation.
legal_tests_applied: The laws of belligerent occupation apply only to an occupation during the course of actual warfare and cease to apply once the enemy has been totally defeated and the conquest is complete.
The principle of territorial supremacy, which grants every state the discretion and legal right to exclude aliens from its territory and to make laws regulating their entry, residence, and eviction.
why_appellant_lost: The court determined that the state of 'occupation' under the Geneva Conventions ends when conquest is followed by subjugation, and therefore the Conventions ceased to apply after December 20, 1961, removing any protection against deportation the appellant might have had.

The Geneva Conventions Act does not create a right or cause of action for a protected person to enforce the Conventions in a municipal court against the government; it only creates an obligation for the government itself.
By refusing Indian nationality and retaining his Portuguese nationality, the appellant legally became a foreigner in India and thus subject to the Foreigners Act.
why_respondent_won: A state exercises territorial supremacy over all persons in its territory and can make laws for regulating the entry, residence, and eviction of aliens. The application of the Foreigners Act to the appellant was therefore legally competent.
The appellant, as a Portuguese national, could only stay in India with a valid permit. Since he did not have one, he was rightly prosecuted under the law applicable to him.

The laws of belligerent occupation, and by extension the protections of the Geneva Convention invoked by the appellant, do not apply after an enemy has been totally defeated and the territory is subjugated.
policy_considerations: If there is no provision of law which the courts can enforce, the court may be powerless and may have to leave the matter to what was described as the 'indignation of mankind'.
